Fiverr acquired us for $92M.

I still run AutoDS inside Fiverr today, and dropshippers on the platform have earned over $1B selling through it.

And I'm still building new products from zero, the same way I built the first one.

I never raised money for it. No investors, no outside capital, at any point in ten years.

The company was profitable from day one, and I still took no salary for the first five years, because everything it made went back into building it.

It grew to 250  employees across 30  countries without a single outside dollar.

So I built software to run them for me.

It was a black screen. No design, no website, nothing anyone else was ever meant to see, and it held every account I had in one place.

That software was AutoDS, years before it had a name or a single user who wasn't me.

So the next morning I opened a new eBay account. 

Then another one, and I kept going until there were 100 of them, created by hand, one at a time.

eBay had already shown me it could take an account away overnight, and I wanted to be sure losing one wouldn't take everything with it again.

By the time I finished, I had 100 accounts and no realistic way to run them.

Then eBay banned it permanently for a policy violation.

7 years of listings, orders, and reputation were gone in a snap of a finger, and there was nothing left of the business that didn't run through that account.

I had no way to sell anything the next morning...

Then I did it again with something else, and again, and it stopped being a thing I was testing.

I ran it for 7 years. Through the end of school and into my 20s, full-time.

Every order, every review, and all the seller reputation I built ran through one eBay account. 

By 21, that account was everything I had.

A few years later, I wanted to buy a phone for myself. 

I found the same phone on a Chinese site for less than it was selling for on eBay. Same product, same photos, same description, different price.

So I copied the listing onto eBay to see what would happen. It sold in three hours. 

Ordered it from the supplier, had it shipped straight to the buyer, and kept the difference.

I wasn't trying to build anything. I just wanted a phone.

At 14, I started selling e-cigarettes at school. Kids asked where mine came from. I told them I could get them one, and they paid me upfront a month before I handed anything over.

I was terrified of speaking in front of people at the time, and I stood in our hallway taking orders anyway.

That was the first thing I ever sold.

I'm Lior.

At 21, eBay permanently banned the account I had spent 7 years building.

The next morning, I opened 100 new accounts and built a tool to run them.

That tool became AutoDS - the company I bootstrapped from 0 to an 8-figure exit.

What I'd add here (as someone who bootstrapped with no investors and sold my company for $92M):

Every founder goes through the same stations.

1. You ship before you feel ready.

You never really feel ready. Waiting for that feeling is how most people lose a year.

2. You get a no.

The market pushes back. A launch nobody notices, a free trial that never converts to paid, a bad review from someone who actually used the product.

3. You break through.

You work your way past the nos, one at a time. Successful products come out of this phase.

4. You get a bigger no.

The next rejection scales with you. Bigger company, bigger stakes, same feeling.

Mine never got any smaller. We got blocked on Shopify. eBay shut our app down over a regulation we hadn't met. The only thing that changed is how fast I get to the next move.

5. You scale aggressively.

You hire faster than you can remember everyone's name. And you bet on those people the same way you bet on the product.

6. New game, next peak.

You fail a level, you clear it, you level up, and the prize is a harder map.

You never stop being on one of these.

If you're between 18 and 25 with a business idea you haven't started, you'll notice this:

- Some of the people around you already know exactly what they want.
- Some are studying something they picked at 17.
- Some took a job and like it.
- Some are waiting until they've saved enough.
- Some are waiting for the right person to build it with.
- Some are watching people their age start things and deciding it's different for them.
- Some already started and stopped.
- Some are waiting to feel ready.

Nobody feels ready. That isn't the signal you think it is.

There's no long-term plan that makes this safe. You just need the first step, and you go from there.

It's a game. You open the map first, and then you figure out what's in it.

You'll feel ready later. Start it now.

Was that discipline? Was I saving for something? Did I have a rule about not spending money on myself?

No. I simply wanted to be ahead of my competitors.

So I used the company balance as my ‘scoreboard.’

It worked for me because it was something that I could gamify. I knew where I was that day, and I knew where I wanted to be a year later.

For some people it’s a car (and that’s fine too). You just have to understand that there’s a big difference between the car you’re saving for and the car you want because you saw someone else driving it. 

You know what yours costs. You have no idea what he paid for his.

So decide for yourself where you want to go.

You can want the car, the watch, the lifestyle... 

Just make sure you're playing your own game.

A stupid simple way to start a SaaS:

Few years ago (at a conference), people asked me how I manage my own business.

I told them I have software that automatically runs 100 eBay accounts for me.

They wondered and asked how they could use it for their own businesses too.

I told them, “It's not open to the public, but let's stay in touch.”

I got their phone numbers. 
Added them to my WhatsApp. 
Saved them as a list: eBay 1, eBay 2, eBay 3.

I started to build the software for them.

I asked them: if I release it, would you use it? They said yes.

We went public with a better version for a few weeks for free, and then straight away started charging.

So if you're starting now:

1. Build a tool that solves your own problem.
2. Talk to people with the same problem.
3. Let them use your solution for free.
5. Build what they ask for.
6. Charge.

You already know your first step. Go do that one.
